claim: The founding lines of the RIAILs were the laboratory strain N2 (Bristol) and the Hawaiian natural isolate CB4856, whose genomes differ at approximately one in ~240 base pairs.
source: The founding lines of the RIAILs were the laboratory strain N2 (Bristol) and the Hawaiian natural isolate CB4856, whose genomes differ at approximately one in ~240 base pairs (Kim et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2019, which provides the genomic difference data.

claim: The panel of 182 RIAILs was generated from ten rounds of random intercrossing, followed by ten rounds of selfing.
source: The panel of 182 RIAILs was generated from ten rounds of random intercrossing, followed by ten rounds of selfing (Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rockman and Kruglyak, 2009, and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 12,000,000 microscopy pictures were obtained from 3D movies of 9,641 embryos.
source: This resulted in a total of ~12,000,000 microscopy pictures from the 3D movies of the 9,641 embryos that were imaged (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and references Figure 1C showing the data.

claim: The founding C. elegans strains N2 and CB4856 had similar spindle characteristics.
source: The founding C. elegans strains used to create the RIAILs, N2 and CB4856, had similar spindle characteristics (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A; Farhadifar et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and citation to Farhadifar et al., 2015.

claim: Extensive quantitative variations in spindle characteristics were observed across the RIAIL panel.
source: In contrast, we observed extensive quantitative variations in spindle characteristics across the RIAIL panel (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C-E).
evidence: The claim is supported by references to multiple figures showing the variation data.

claim: Statistically significant broad-sense heritability was found for all spindle traits.
source: We found statistically significant broad-sense heritability (the fraction of variance due to differences between lines) for all spindle traits (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B; Lynch and Walsh, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3B showing the heritability data and citation to Lynch and Walsh, 1998 for the methodology.

claim: There is a negligible correlation between initial and final spindle length across the RIAILs (p = 0.17).
source: To test this prediction, we plotted the average final spindle length vs the average initial spindle length for each of the RIAILs and instead observed a negligible correlation between these two (Figure 2B, p = 0.17).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p-value) and reference to Figure 2B showing the correlation data.

claim: A Timer model does not explain final spindle length in C. elegans.
source: Thus, a Timer model does not explain final spindle length in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of correlation between initial and final spindle length, which contradicts Timer model predictions.

claim: Final spindle length is highly correlated with cell area across the RIAIL panel (p = 2.97E-36).
source: To test this possibility, we plotted final spindle length as a function of the area of the cell measured from DIC images, which is a proxy for cell volume because of the rotational symmetry of the embryo, across the RIAIL panel, and observed a highly significant correlation (Figure 2D, p = 2.97E-36).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p-value) and reference to Figure 2D showing the correlation.

claim: Cell area is highly correlated with cell length across the RIAILs (p = 8.38E-73).
source: However, cell area is highly correlated with cell length across the RIAILs (Figure 2E, p = 8.38E-73)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p-value) and reference to Figure 2E showing the correlation.

claim: There is a negligible partial correlation between final spindle length and cell area conditioned on cell length (p = 0.13).
source: Doing this, we observed a negligible partial correlation between the final spindle length and cell area conditioned on cell length across the RIAILs (Figure 2F, p = 0.13).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p-value) and reference to Figure 2F showing the partial correlation data.

claim: Cell volume does not determine final spindle length.
source: Therefore, cell volume does not determine final spindle length, which is inconsistent with the simplest version of the Limiting Component model considered here.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of partial correlation between cell area and final spindle length when conditioned on cell length.

claim: Cell length is a critical factor in the regulation of final spindle length in C. elegans.
source: Our analysis so far indicates that cell length is a critical factor in the regulation of final spindle length in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation analyses showing cell length's importance while cell volume is not independently important.

claim: Final spindle length is highly correlated with cell length across the RIAIL panel (p = 7.96E-55).
source: To test these predictions, we plot the final spindle length as a function of cell length across the RIAIL panel and find that they are highly correlated as predicted (Figure 2H, p = 7.96E-55).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p-value) and reference to Figure 2H showing the correlation.

claim: Final spindle length is positively correlated with centrosome distance (p = 6.81E-14).
source: However, final spindle length was also positively correlated with centrosome distance (Figure 2I, p = 6.81E-14)
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis (p-value) and reference to Figure 2I showing the correlation.

claim: The simplest Boundary model does not explain the regulation of final spindle length in C. elegans.
source: Thus, the simplest Boundary model does not explain the regulation of final spindle length in C. elegans.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the positive correlation between final spindle length and centrosome distance, which contradicts the Boundary model prediction.

claim: QTL1 on chromosome III was identified through conditional QTL mapping of final spindle length conditioned on cell length.
source: This conditional QTL mapping revealed one QTL on chromosome III, which we refer to as QTL1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by QTL mapping analysis and reference to Figure 3A showing the QTL location.

claim: QTL2 on chromosome III was identified by conditioning final length on both cell length and QTL1.
source: Similar to above, we conditioned final length on both cell length and QTL1, which revealed an additional QTL on chromosome III that we refer to as QTL2 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by QTL mapping analysis and reference to Figure 3B showing the QTL location.

claim: QTL1 explains 21% of the variation in final spindle length that is independent of cell length.
source: QTL1 explains 21% of the variation across the RIAILs (i.e. heritability) in final spindle length that is independent of the cell length, while QTL2 explains an additional 10%.
evidence: The claim is supported by heritability analysis from the QTL mapping data.

claim: QTL2 explains an additional 10% of the variation in final spindle length independent of cell length and QTL1.
source: QTL1 explains 21% of the variation across the RIAILs (i.e. heritability) in final spindle length that is independent of the cell length, while QTL2 explains an additional 10%.
evidence: The claim is supported by heritability analysis from the QTL mapping data.

claim: Lines with the N2 allele of QTL1 have shorter final spindles.
source: Lines with the N2 allele of QTL1 have shorter final spindles (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3C showing the phenotypic data for different alleles.

claim: Lines with the N2 allele of QTL2 have longer final spindles.
source: while lines with the N2 allele of QTL2 have longer final spindles (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 3D showing the phenotypic data for different alleles.

claim: The N2 alleles of QTL1 and QTL2 have opposite effects on final spindle length.
source: Thus, the N2 alleles of QTL1 and QTL2 have opposite effects on final spindle length (as do the CB4856 alleles).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that N2 allele of QTL1 shortens spindles while N2 allele of QTL2 lengthens them.

claim: QTL1 overlapped with the location of gpr-1, which contains two missense variants that differ between N2 and CB4856.
source: QTL1 overlapped with the location of gpr-1, which contains two missense variants (nonsynonymous) that differ between N2 and CB4856 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing the variant locations.

claim: GPR-1 regulates pulling forces on astral MTs that drive spindle oscillations, positioning, and elongation.
source: GPR-1 regulates pulling forces on astral MTs that drive spindle oscillations, positioning, and elongation (Hara and Kimura, 2009; Pecreaux et al., 2006; Colombo et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: gpr-1/2 (RNAi) embryos have shorter final spindle length (FL = 17.4±0.2 μm, p = 3.82E-30).
source: Consistent with previous results (Hara and Kimura, 2009), we observed that gpr-1/2 (RNAi) embryos have shorter final spindle length (FL = 17.4±0.2 [μm], p = 3.82E-30, Figure 3E, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance and references to Figure 3E and video.

claim: QTL2 overlapped with the location of par-2, which contains three missense and two synonymous variants between N2 and CB4856.
source: QTL2 overlapped with the location of par-2, one of the central components of the PAR system in C. elegans (Cuenca et al., 2003), which contains three missense (nonsynonymous) and two synonymous variants between N2 and CB4856 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by genomic analysis and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing the variant locations.

claim: Lines with the N2 allele of QTL2 have significantly higher PAR-2 transcript abundance than lines with the CB4856 allele (p = 6.08E-17).
source: We analyzed previously obtained data from the same panel of RIAILs (Rockman et al., 2010) and found that lines with the N2 allele of QTL2 have significantly higher PAR-2 transcript abundance than lines with the CB4856 allele (p = 6.08E-17, Figure 3—figure supplement 3
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of transcript data with statistical significance and reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: par-2 (RNAi) embryos have shorter final spindle length (FL = 19.8±0.2 μm, p = 1.03E-22).
source: par-2 (RNAi) embryos have shorter final spindle length (FL = 19.8±0.2 [μm], p = 1.03E-22, Figure 3F, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements with statistical significance and references to Figure 3F and video.

claim: PAR-2 regulates final spindle length.
source: While prior work has described the role of PAR-2 in regulating spindle positioning (Grill et al., 2001), this RNAi knockdown shows that PAR-2 also regulates final spindle length.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the RNAi knockdown experiment showing reduced spindle length, and is contrasted with prior knowledge about PAR-2's role in positioning.

claim: After cup-cut ablation parallel to the spindle axis, centrosomes moved toward the cell periphery with an average speed of 14.5±2.8 μm/min.
source: We performed this pattern of ablation on 13 embryos (Figure 4C) and found that the average speed of centrosome motion after the cut was 14.5±2.8 μm/min
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements from 13 embryos and reference to Figure 4C.

claim: After cup-cut ablation parallel to the spindle axis, centrosomes moved an average of 3.9±0.2 μm toward the cell periphery.
source: and that the centrosomes moved an average of 3.9±0.2 μm toward the cell periphery.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements from the cup-cut ablation experiments.

claim: Astral MTs on one side of the centrosome are subject to net pulling forces, not a balance of pushing and pulling forces.
source: The rapid motion of the centrosome in the direction of the remaining MTs after the cup-cut indicates that there is not a balance of pushing and pulling forces acting on these MTs, rather, they are subject to net pulling forces (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the laser ablation experiment results showing centrosome movement after cup-cut.

claim: After plane-cut through the spindle, the average speed of centrosome motion was 1.6±1.0 μm/min.
source: We performed this pattern of ablation on 15 embryos (Figure 4G) and found that the average speed of centrosome motion after the cut was 1.6±1.0 μm/min
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements from 15 embryos and reference to Figure 4G.

claim: After plane-cut through the spindle, centrosomes moved an average of 0.7±0.1 μm toward the cell periphery.
source: and that the centrosomes moved an average of 0.7±0.1 μm toward the cell periphery.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements from the plane-cut ablation experiments.

claim: Forces from the spindle have a relatively minor impact on the final position of the centrosomes in C. elegans.
source: This result argues that forces from the spindle have a relatively minor impact on the final position of the centrosomes in C. elegans (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the small centrosome displacement after spindle plane-cut ablation.

claim: spd-1 (RNAi) embryos lack a central spindle in anaphase.
source: To further test this conclusion, we studied spd-1 (RNAi) embryos, which lack a central spindle in anaphase (Figure 4I, inset) (Verbrugghe and White, 2004)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Verbrugghe and White, 2004, and reference to Figure 4I inset showing the phenotype.

claim: spd-1 (RNAi) embryos have nearly identical final spindle length to controls (24.5±0.1 μm vs 23.8±0.2 μm, p = 2.2E-3).
source: and found that their final spindle length is nearly identical to controls (24.5±0.1 μm for spd-1 (RNAi) vs 23.8±0.2 μm for control, p = 2.2E-3) (Figure 4I, Figure 4—video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements with statistical analysis and references to Figure 4I and video.

claim: The central spindle has only a very minor impact on final spindle length.
source: Thus, the central spindle has only a very minor impact on final spindle length.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spd-1 (RNAi) experiment showing similar final spindle length despite lack of central spindle.

claim: After perpendicular cup-cut, the average speed of centrosome motion was 22.3±4.3 μm/min.
source: We performed this pattern of ablation on 15 embryos (Figure 4L) and found that the average speed of centrosome motion after the cut was 22.3±4.3 μm/min
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements from 15 embryos and reference to Figure 4L.

claim: After perpendicular cup-cut, centrosomes moved an average of 6.6±0.3 μm toward the cell periphery.
source: and that the centrosomes moved an average of 6.6±0.3 μm toward the cell periphery.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements from the perpendicular cup-cut ablation experiments.

claim: There are pulling forces present both parallel and perpendicular to the spindle axis even when centrosome motion has ceased.
source: Thus, even when centrosome motion has ceased, and the spindle has obtained its final length at the end of anaphase, there are pulling forces present both parallel (Figure 4B) and perpendicular (Figure 4K) to the spindle axis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the results of both parallel and perpendicular cup-cut experiments showing centrosome movement.

claim: The final length of the spindle is determined by a balance of pulling forces acting in different directions on centrosomes.
source: This observation is consistent with the hypothesis that the final length of the spindle is determined by a balance of pulling forces acting in different directions on centrosomes (Figure 4M).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the laser ablation experiments showing pulling forces in multiple directions.

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, only one MT can bind a CFG at a time due to stoichiometric interactions.
source: Due to the stoichiometric nature of the interaction between molecular motors and MTs, only one MT can bind a CFG at a time.
evidence: The claim is based on known biochemical properties of molecular motors and MTs.

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model simulations, centrosomes initially located near the cell center separate and move to a final position along the long axis of the cell at a finite distance from the cell surface.
source: Centrosomes initially located near the cell center, separate, and move to a final position along the long axis of the cell, at a finite distance from the cell surface (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, centrosomes always move to the same final positions regardless of starting position.
source: We repeated this simulation with centrosomes starting from different positions and found that centrosomes always move to the same final positions (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, cortical pulling forces stably position centrosomes.
source: Thus, in the Stoichiometric Model, a balance of pulling forces stably positions centrosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the simulation results showing stable centrosome positioning.

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, centrosomes stably position irrespective of the number of CFGs, even with 100,000 CFGs (ten times more than MTs).
source: The centrosomes stably positioned irrespective of the number of CFGs -- even for simulations with 100,000 CFGs, ten times more CFGs than MTs (the largest number of CFGs we investigated, Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results testing various numbers of CFGs.

claim: A limited number of CFGs does not explain the stable positioning of centrosomes in the Stoichiometric Model.
source: Thus, a limited number of CFGs does not explain the stable positioning of centrosomes in our model.
evidence: The claim is inferred from simulation results showing stable positioning even with many more CFGs than MTs.

claim: In simulations without stoichiometric interactions, centrosome positions are always unstable and centrosomes migrate until they contact the cell periphery.
source: In these simulations, the centrosome's positions are always unstable, and the centrosomes migrate until they contact the cell periphery (Figure 5—figure supplement 3; Materials and methods).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Stoichiometric interactions prevent the destabilizing feedback that occurs in the absence of stoichiometry.
source: Stoichiometric interactions prevent this destabilizing feedback.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing simulations with and without stoichiometric interactions.

claim: The stoichiometric interaction of MTs and CFGs allows cortical pulling forces to stably position centrosomes.
source: Thus, the stoichiometric interaction of MTs and CFGs allows cortical pulling forces to stably position centrosomes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of simulations with and without stoichiometric interactions.

claim: Cortical pulling forces with stoichiometric interactions are stabilizing even when the number of CFGs are greater than the number of MTs.
source: Cortical pulling forces with stoichiometric interactions are stabilizing even when the number of CFGs are greater than the number of MTs.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results testing various CFG numbers.

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, two centrosomes compete for CFGs between them.
source: This effect is evident in our simulations, where the probabilities of attachment of CFGs from one centrosome are reduced by the presence of a second centrosome (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) because two centrosomes compete for the CFGs between them.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: In simulations, removing one centrosome allows the remaining centrosome to move to the cell center.
source: A consequence of this competition is that removing one centrosome in the simulation allows the remaining centrosome to interact more strongly with CFGs at the center of the cell, which thus moves the centrosome to the cell center (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figures 6A and B.

claim: After laser ablation of one centrosome, the remaining centrosome moved to the cell center in experiments.
source: After ablation of one centrosome, the other centrosome moved to the cell center (Figure 6D, Figure 6—video 1). We repeated this experiment for 13 embryos and observed a consistent centering of the remaining centrosome (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental results from 13 embryos shown in Figures 6D and 6E and video.

claim: The presence of one centrosome modulates the forces acting on the other centrosome.
source: The agreement between simulations and experiment strongly argues that the presence of one centrosome modulates the forces acting on the other centrosome, which is a key prediction of the Stoichiometric Model.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the agreement between simulation predictions and experimental results of single centrosome ablation.

claim: The posterior side of the cortex in C. elegans has ~50% more CFGs than the anterior side.
source: Previous studies in C. elegans have shown that the posterior side of the cortex has ~50% more CFGs than the anterior side (Grill et al., 2003; Redemann et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Simulations with asymmetric CFG distribution accurately reproduce the dynamics of spindle elongation.
source: These simulations with an asymmetric distribution of CFGs accurately reproduce the dynamics of spindle elongation (Figure 7C)
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Simulations with asymmetric CFG distribution accurately reproduce spindle positioning.
source: and spindle positioning (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In par-6 (RNAi) embryos, the spindle positioned in the middle of the cell and obtained the same final spindle length as controls in both experiments and simulations.
source: In both experiments and simulations, the spindle positioned in the middle of the cell and obtained the same final spindle length as controls (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental and simulation results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In simulations, spindles in smaller cells have a slower rate of elongation, reach a smaller final length, and position less asymmetrically.
source: In these simulations, spindles in smaller cells have a slower rate of elongation, reach a smaller final length, and position less asymmetrically (Figure 7G and H).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figures 7G and H.

claim: The Stoichiometric Model reproduces the scaling of final spindle length with cell length observed across the RIAILs (regression coefficient = 0.52±0.02 for theory vs 0.47±0.02 for RIAILs, p = 0.08).
source: This model reproduces the scaling of final spindle length with cell length observed across the RIAILs (Figure 7I, red, theory, regression coefficient = 0.52±0.02; light blue, RIAILs, regression coefficient = 0.47±0.02, p = 0.08).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The scaling of final spindle length in simulations is in quantitative agreement with scaling across natural isolates (regression coefficient = 0.46±0.05, p = 0.27).
source: The scaling of final spindle length in the simulations is also in quantitative agreement with its scaling across natural isolates and across different species (Figure 7I, dark blue, natural isolates, regression coefficient = 0.46±0.05, p = 0.27
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The scaling of final spindle length in simulations is in quantitative agreement with scaling across nematode species (regression coefficient = 0.57±0.10, p = 0.62).
source: purple, nematode species, regression coefficient = 0.57±0.10, p = 0.62).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 7I.

claim: The Stoichiometric Model reproduces the scaling of centrosome distance from the cortex with cell length, the scaling of the final position of spindle center with cell length, and the scaling of the elongation rate with cell length across RIAILs, natural isolates, and nematode species.
source: The Stoichiometric Model also reproduces the scaling of centrosome distance from the cortex with cell length, the scaling of the final position of spindle center with cell length, and the scaling of the elongation rate with cell length across RIAILs, natural isolates, and nematode species (Figure 7J).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of simulation and experimental data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: The Stoichiometric Model explains the scaling of spindle traits both within and between species.
source: Thus, the Stoichiometric Model explains the scaling of spindle traits both within and between species.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the quantitative agreement between model predictions and experimental data across multiple datasets.

claim: Spindle elongation and asymmetric positioning in C. elegans are driven by cortical pulling forces acting unevenly on the two centrosomes.
source: Previous studies have shown that spindle elongation and asymmetric positioning in C. elegans are driven by cortical pulling forces acting unevenly on the two centrosomes (Grill et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Laser ablation experiments and genetic perturbations show that spindle elasticity and pushing forces do not significantly contribute to the final position of centrosomes in C. elegans embryos.
source: Our laser ablation experiments and genetic perturbations show that spindle elasticity and pushing forces do not significantly contribute to the final position of centrosomes in C. elegans embryos.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing minimal centrosome movement after spindle ablation and similar spindle length in spd-1 (RNAi).

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, each CFG can only bind one MT at a time and every MT that is attached to a CFG experiences the same magnitude of pulling force, irrespective of the MT's length.
source: In this model, each CFG can only bind one MT at a time (i.e. the interactions are stoichiometric), and every MT that is attached to a CFG, experiences the same magnitude of pulling force, irrespective of the MT's length.
evidence: The claim describes the fundamental assumptions of the Stoichiometric Model based on known biochemical properties.

claim: In the Stoichiometric Model, the stable positioning of centrosomes results from the stoichiometric interaction between MTs and CFGs, which prevents the destabilizing feedback present in previous models.
source: In this model, the stable positioning of centrosomes results from the stoichiometric interaction between MTs and CFGs, which prevents the destabilizing feedback present in previous models of cortical pulling forces.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of model behavior with and without stoichiometric interactions.

claim: Cortical pulling forces are sufficient to stably position centrosomes even in the absence of explicit length dependent forces or a limiting number of CFGs.
source: Thus, cortical pulling forces are sufficient to stably position centrosomes even in the absence of explicit length dependent forces or a limiting number of CFGs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the simulation results showing stable positioning under various conditions.

claim: The Stoichiometric Model quantitatively explains the asymmetry in positioning of the spindle center by an uneven distribution of CFGs between the anterior and posterior halves of the embryo.
source: The Stoichiometric Model quantitatively explains the asymmetry in positioning of the spindle center by an uneven distribution of CFGs between the anterior and posterior halves of the embryo.
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation results showing asymmetric positioning with asymmetric CFG distribution.

claim: The Stoichiometric Model quantitatively reproduces the correlations between spindles and cell length observed across recombinant inbred lines, natural isolates, and nematode species.
source: The Stoichiometric Model we developed quantitatively reproduces these correlations.
evidence: The claim is supported by the quantitative agreement between model predictions and experimental data across multiple datasets.

claim: The Stoichiometric Model provides a mechanistic explanation for the evolution of the spindle in nematodes.
source: This provides a mechanistic explanation for the evolution of the spindle in nematodes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the model's ability to reproduce evolutionary patterns of spindle variation.

claim: The study characterized variations in spindles across ~100 C. elegans natural isolates and ~40 additional nematode species spanning over 100 million years of evolution.
source: In a previous study (Farhadifar et al., 2015), we characterized the first mitotic division in ~100 C. elegans natural isolates and ~40 additional nematode species and discovered extensive variations in spindles, both within and between species.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Variations in all aspects of spindles investigated were correlated with cell length across natural isolates and nematode species.
source: Variations in all aspects of spindles we investigated were correlated with cell length.
evidence: The claim is based on prior work cited in the manuscript.

claim: Cell length is subject to stabilizing selection, which is sufficient to explain variations in spindles within and between species due to correlations between spindle traits and cell length.
source: We found evidence that cell length is subject to stabilizing selection, which, due to the correlation of spindle traits with cell length, is sufficient to explain the variations in spindles within and between species.
evidence: The claim is based on prior work and evolutionary analysis cited in the manuscript.

claim: The correlations between spindles and cell length across recombinant inbred lines are the same as the correlations across natural isolates and nematode species.
source: As part of the present study, we investigated the correlations between spindles and cell length across the recombinant inbred lines and found that they are the same as the correlations across natural isolates and nematode species.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of correlation data across different datasets.

claim: The first cell division in C. elegans is asymmetric with two daughter cells having different sizes and fates.
source: The first cell division in C. elegans is asymmetric: the two daughter cells have different sizes and fates.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about C. elegans development.

claim: The asymmetry of the single-cell C. elegans embryo is established shortly after fertilization, with the cell cortex divided into two domains enriched in either anterior or posterior PARs.
source: The asymmetry of the single-cell embryo is established shortly after fertilization, with the cell cortex divided into two domains enriched in either anterior or posterior partitioning-defected proteins (PARs) (Kemphues et al., 1988).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The spindle forms in the center of the C. elegans embryo and is a bipolar structure primarily composed of transitory microtubules and their associated proteins, with centrosomes localized at each pole.
source: The spindle forms in the center of the embryo, and is a bipolar structure primarily composed of transitory microtubules and their associated proteins, with centrosomes localized at each pole.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about spindle structure.

claim: Subsequent elongation and asymmetric positioning of the spindle is driven by factors, asymmetrically localized by the PAR proteins, which exert pulling forces on astral microtubules.
source: Subsequent elongation and asymmetric positioning of the spindle is driven by factors, asymmetrically localized by the PAR proteins, which exert pulling forces on astral microtubules (Colombo et al., 2003; Grill et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The C. elegans embryo divides asymmetrically due to the asymmetric positioning of the spindle.
source: The embryo then divides asymmetrically due to the asymmetric positioning of the spindle.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about C. elegans cell division.

claim: Spindle size scales with cell size across multiple organisms.
source: Recently, several groups have investigated variations of this machinery with cell size, finding that spindle size scales with cell size (Brown et al., 2007; Brust-Mascher et al., 2004; Decker et al., 2018; Good et al., 2013; Greenan et al., 2010; Hara and Kimura, 2009; Hazel et al., 2013; Loughlin et al., 2011; Reber et al., 2013; Wilbur and Heald, 2013; Lacroix et al., 2018; Rizk et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Many aspects of cell division change with cell size, including the dynamics and positioning of the spindle, reorganization of organelles and the cytoplasm, and rearrangements of the cortex.
source: Many other aspects of cell division also change with cell size, including the dynamics and positioning of the spindle, reorganization of organelles and the cytoplasm, and rearrangements of the cortex that ultimately result in the division of the cell (Hara and Kimura, 2009; Hara and Kimura, 2011; Blanchoud et al., 2015; Carvalho et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The mechanisms by which cell division processes change in a coordinated fashion over development and evolution are poorly understood.
source: The mechanisms by which these processes change in a coordinated fashion over development and evolution are poorly understood.
evidence: The claim represents a knowledge gap in the field based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: The Stoichiometric Model accounts for variations in all the spindle traits studied across nematode species spanning over 100 million years of evolution.
source: This model accounts for variations in all the spindle traits we studied here, both within species and across nematode species spanning over 100 million years of evolution.
evidence: The claim is supported by the quantitative agreement between model predictions and experimental data across evolutionary timescales.
